On November 29, 1889, Assistant Engineer Reginald Shaw wrote a field dispatch from Chanda to the Chief Engineer in Calcutta regarding the survey of the Bengal Nagpur railway extension.

This is a field dispatch from the survey of the Bengal Nagpur railway extension, written at Chanda on 29 November 1889 by the assistant engineer, Mr. Reginald Shaw, to the chief engineer at Calcutta. Shaw reports that his survey party, numbering 34 persons, including 12 chainmen and 6 sappers of the Madras Sappers, had completed the location survey of the 92-mile section from Nagbhid to Chanda on 22 November after fourteen weeks in the field. The line as located follows the Wyne Ganga valley for 41 miles, crosses that river by a bridge of seven spans of 150 feet at Karanja, and then takes the northern flank of the hills.

Shaw estimates earthwork for the whole section at 480,000 cubic yards, of which 62,000 cubic yards are rock excavation occurring in the eleven miles beyond Ballarshah. Three alignments were examined for the Karanja crossing; the adopted line is 1.7 miles longer than the southern route but avoids 90,000 cubic yards of rock and two well sinkings. He reports the country between Ballarshah and Chanda to be healthy except in the months of July and August, when fever this season carried off four chainmen. The party's expenses to date were 19,400 rupees against a sanctioned grant of 30,000 rupees. Shaw requests an additional 8,000 rupees for the next season, a theodolite to replace the one damaged at the Wyne Ganga crossing on 3 September, and the loan of a second survey elephant from the Chanda division because the party's own elephant had gone lame after the monsoon. He closes by noting that the levelling of the first 40 miles has been checked twice and agrees within 0.15 feet.

The consulate report on the wool trade of the La Plata region was drawn up at Buenos Aires by Her Majesty's Consul, Mr. Edmund Monson, and was forwarded to the Foreign Office on 20 April 1875. It records that the clip of the season just closed was estimated at 68,000,000 pounds weight, against 61,000,000 pounds in the previous season, the increase being chiefly assigned to the extension of fencing on the estancias of the southern camps. Of this clip, some 26,000 bales were shipped to Havre, 19,000 bales to Antwerp, and 11,500 bales to Great Britain, the remainder being worked up in the local factories, of which fourteen were reported in operation against nine a year before.

The average price realized at the sales was elevenpence per pound greasy, a fall of twopence farthing on the year. The consul notes that the S.A. Bienvenida sheep, introduced by the Sociedad Rural in 1868, now numbered, by the best estimates, 3,000,000 head, and that their wool brought a premium of one penny per pound over the common criollo clip. Freight to London was taken at five eighths of a penny per pound, and to Havre at a halfpenny farthing; insurance on London account ran at thirty-five shillings percent. The report concludes with the observation that the drainage of the flooding lands near Dolores, begun in 1873 under the engineer Mr. James Baine, had reclaimed some 400 square miles of pasture, and that the railway from Tandil to the port, opened on 1 February of the present year, had already reduced cartage charges by two shillings per bale.

This text is a log of the 1866 Davis Strait fishery voyage of the *Diana*, a 350-ton register brig-rigged steam whaler from Hull. The log was maintained by the ship's surgeon, Dr. Charles Edward Smith.

Under the command of Captain John Gravill, the *Diana* departed Hull on February 12 with a crew of 49. This crew included eight inexperienced "green hands" who were paid two pounds ten shillings per month, while the experienced sailors earned three pounds five shillings. The ship crossed the Arctic circle on March 3 at longitude 22 degrees west and reached the ice edge off Disko on March 19.

The crew struck their first whale on April 2 off the Women's Islands, which provided 9 hundredweight of bone and 12 tons of oil. A second whale, taken on April 17, yielded 15 tons of oil. By the end of May, the total catch consisted of 1,400 seals and four whales.

On June 11, the ship lost its rudder after being nipped in the ice in Melville Bay. Within three days, the carpenter constructed a temporary rudder using spare spars. The ship then became beset and drifted with the ice pack for 61 days. During this time, Dr. Smith recorded the first case of scurvy on July 8, and by mid-August, 22 men were on the sick list. Because the ship had run out of lime juice, the crew gathered and ate sorrel from the Greenland coast when the ship touched land on August 21. Three men died during the final week of August and were buried on shore.

The *Diana* broke free from the ice on September 25 and returned to Hull on October 11. The voyage yielded 3 tons of bone and 41 tons of oil; however, the voyage was only profitable due to the seal catch. The ship's owners, Samuel and Charles Gourlay, reported gross earnings of 3,860 pounds and paid each seasoned crew member 19 pounds twelve shillings for the voyage.
